FinanceTab.title: US trade regulator and 22 states accuse Amazon of taking $20bn with secret surcharges
FinanceTab.text:
The US’s main trade regulator and 22 states sued Amazon on Monday, alleging the online retailer “secretly and systematically overcharged” advertisers on Amazon.com.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said these practices led to higher costs for customers on items like groceries and other essential goods that are sold on Amazon.

“Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices. These higher costs were largely passed on to American consumers,” said Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair.

The agency accused the company of taking in more than $20bn from “hidden surcharges”, in what it deems an “ad-rigging scheme”. Amazon’s advertising business has grown significantly in recent years, becoming the third-largest online advertising marketplace after Google and Meta. The FTC says Amazon generates more than $68bn in ad revenue on its website.

The lawsuit alleges that 1.2 million advertising customers were overcharged since 2019, including more than 500,000 small- and medium-sized businesses.

An Amazon spokesperson pointed the Guardian to a blog post the company published in response to the legal action, which calls the legal action a “misguided lawsuit”.

“Amazon strongly disagrees,” the post reads.

The government’s case hinges on Amazon’s advertising auction system, called “second-price auctions”, that lets the winning bidder pay only slightly more than the second-highest bid. Regulators allege that with this system, Amazon could secretly raise the second-highest bids with a higher “shill” bid of its own.

“We believe Amazon manipulated its ad auctions to inflate what sellers had to pay, adding billions of dollars in costs that ultimately get passed on to customers with higher prices,” said Jeff Jackson, the attorney general for North Carolina, one of the states involved in the suit.

The suit alleges Amazon tested how much it could increase the amount it charges without advertisers flinching. Internal documents show one manager allegedly describing the company’s pricing strategy as “hoping that advertisers don’t notice and decrease bids or ad spend”.

Amazon denied these allegations and said the company gives “customers the lowest prices every day across the widest selection of products”.

“After reviewing approximately 1.5 million pages spanning six years, the FTC leans on a handful of simplified communications to allege a companywide effort to deceive,” Amazon wrote in its blog post. “That is patently false.”

Rob Bonta, the attorney general for California, noted in a press conference that the lawsuit arises from a partnership between conservative states, liberal ones, and the federal government. He said this lawsuit is focusing on Amazon’s alleged unlawful activities and its deception around those practices.

“Amazon’s price inflation is illegal, plain and simple,” Bonta said. “This is a massive corporation. They can be wildly successful and also follow the law.”

The federal agency and states are asking the court to bar Amazon from continuing the allegedly deceptive advertising practices, along with paying civil penalties and refunding advertisers.

FinanceTab.title: As US-Canada tensions flare, who’s calling the shots in Trump’s trade team?
FinanceTab.text:
Having reportedly read Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, in French, during a military tour of duty in Iraq, Jamieson Greer considered himself an unlikely target for accusations of francophobia.

But Donald Trump’s US trade representative, hitherto one of the president’s less high-profile cabinet members, found himself in that uncomfortable position amid the acrimonious collapse of bilateral trade talks with Canada that now threatens to degenerate into an all-out trade war between the two close trading partners whose economies are tightly intertwined.

An apparent pending deal between Washington and Ottawa aimed at avoiding damaging tit-for-tat tariffs broke down at the last minute, with Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, claiming his country had come “under attack” from the US.

Among the multiple and complex points of disagreement was a Canadian accusation that US negotiators had pressed for a weakening of legal protections for the French language, which is most heavily spoken in the province of Quebec.

Canadian provisions include legislation that mandates streaming and online video companies to invest in and promote Canadian content and promote the French language. Carney cast US objections to such regulations as a deal-breaker, and said they amounted to “threats to French language and culture”.

For Greer, a fluent French speaker who once served as a Mormon missionary in Belgium, France and Luxembourg, the charge was too much. “I speak French, too,” he told CNBC, dismissing the claims as “a funny, fake story”.

“My kids speak French,” he said. “One of my kids was born in Paris. So I like the Québécois, and I like that they speak French. What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada.”

The controversy may be the closest glimpse the public will see of Greer being rattled. By Thursday, in what was being being seen by some Canadian officials as a potential olive branch, he was peddling a softer line on the language issue.

“President Trump, myself and the US government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada,” he told CBC, the Canadian broadcaster. “We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important, and we actually champion the use of French.”

The impact was undermined hours later, however, when Trump publicly signed a retributive executive order supposedly changing the name of Lake Ontario – one of the Great Lakes which has shores on both countries – to Lake America. Petty as the act was, it seemed to graphically illustrate the limited freedom of manoeuvre held by anyone representing a president so preoccupied with trade.

And Greer is not the only official seeking to steer the president’s aggressive agenda on trade – raising questions over who is really in control.

Moving the goalposts

Those who have met and worked with Greer describe the 46-year-old – who served as a military lawyer in Iraq, where he is reported to have read Hugo’s classic novel between bombardments – as a model of calm and expertise.

“I have high respect for him. He been pretty creative in terms of trying to thread the needle with other countries as he tries to promote Trump’s trade policies,” said Wendy Cutler, a former US trade representative’s negotiator who has met Greer several times. “From a professional viewpoint, he’s extremely impressive. His reputation as being very level-headed, a very calm demeanor, and not someone who loses his temper or who grandstands.”

It is not known if Greer retained his sang-froid in private as the talks with Canada unravelled, just days after Trump himself publicly declared a deal was at hand.

According to reports, the agreement was derailed after Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, objected to the scale of proposed tariffs reductions on imports of Canadian steel, aluminium and cars, sectors falling under his responsibility after Trump declared them areas of national security under the 1962 Trade Expansion Act.

Carney, explaining why Canada decided to abandon the talks, pointed to disunity among the US negotiators. The White House has denied claims of division between Greer and Lutnick, but seasoned commentators are skeptical.

“Lutnick viewed all this as his turf, and here is Greer, who is the designated guy to be effectively the trade minister, if you think about it in the context of other countries, conducting the negotiations,” said William Reinsch, a senior adviser to the Center for Strategic and International Studies and a former undersecretary for commerce. “It appears Greer was willing to go farther than Lutnick was.

“From the Canadian point of view, this was a disagreement that developed late in the day and led the Canadians to believe that the United States was moving the goalposts.”

Cutler, who served Republican and Democratic administrations during a 27-year stint as a US trade negotiator, said tensions within negotiating teams were not unprecedented, but were normally ironed out before talks reached the critical stage.

“I think the challenge under this administration is that you have Greer in charge of the trade portfolio, but Lutnick’s in charge of section 232 investigations [restricting foreign import on national security grounds] and that’s where a lot of the sensitive issues are,” said Cutler, now vice-president of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

Greer cut his trade negotiating teeth as chief of staff to Robert Lighthizer, US trade representative in Trump’s first presidency, who played the leading role in renegotiating Washington’s economic ties with Mexico and Canada, and the former North America Free Trade Agreement (Nafta), which was replaced with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) in 2020.

He was chosen for the position when Lighthizer apparently indicated he did not wish to be considered for the post a second time. “Greer plays the same role that Lighthizer played,” said Reinsch, who noted, however, that Greer lacked his former boss’s intimate understanding of Congress.

“He figures out legal ways to do what Trump wants to do, and to get as much of Trump’s objectives accomplished as is possible within the framework that he has to operate in,” added Reinsch. “So that allows him to come back to Trump on occasion and say, ‘there’s a better way to get what you want than what you’ve employed so far.”

Another complicating element may be Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing.

He is reckoned by analysts to be a “Trump whisperer” on Canada, despite a belief that his influence has been marginalized compared with the first Trump presidency, when it was widely joked, according to Reinsch, that Lighthizer was reluctant to travel outside Washington for fear that Navarro would persuade the president to adopt impractical trade policies in his absence.

Navarro, who went to jail for contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with a subpoena from the committee investigating the 6 January 2021 insurrection, vented in an appearance on the C-Span network last week.

Asked to respond to an article in the Guardian by the Canadian writer Jen Gerson, who wrote that US retaliation should be taken as a warning by other western allies, Navarro said: “Madam, your country screws us. You’re in bed with the Chinese and playing games with us.

“Look in the mirror at your tariffs codes. You are the problem.”

Navarro has voiced concern that Canada has allowed the import of nearly 50,000 Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles under a most favoured nation agreement, which he fears will ultimately end up crossing the border to be sold in the US.

“Navarro’s worried that the whole USMCA negotiation is really about how do we prevent Canada and Mexico from being a backdoor to Chinese stuff,” Reinsch said. “He would probably have argued last week that the deal wasn’t any good because it wouldn’t shut down Chinese imports in the United States.”

Yet the focus on Trump’s advisers cannot obscure the president’s own fixation with tariffs. Carney referred to agreements being “signed in pencil”, suggesting that Trump would try to change terms even after the details had been hammered out.

“The larger Canadian objection was not due to interagency American disagreement,” Reinsch said. “Trump has very strong fixed views on trade. He thinks tariffs are good. So if you’re going to blame somebody, don’t blame Lutnick or Greer. Blame Trump, because I’m quite confident he had the last word on this.”

Regardless of where blame is apportioned, the consequences of Carney’s defiance will reverberate beyond Canada, analysts say, as other countries forced to confront Trump’s threats of tariffs reassess and recalibrate how they should respond.

“Other countries are watching the developments with Canada very closely,” said Cutler. “Some of our other trading partners have expressed similar frustrations [to the Canadians] to me privately, and so we could be at a turning point.

“It is possible that what we’re experiencing with Canada now spreads to other countries.”

FinanceTab.title: ‘Revenge of the Rust belt’: Starbucks film-maker on Baristas vs Billionaires
FinanceTab.text:
As the food service industry was pushed on to the frontlines of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021, workers at Starbucks stores in the Buffalo region of New York went public to announce their union-organizing campaign.

Their efforts, and Starbucks’ responses, have culminated in one of the most expansive union-organizing campaigns – and one of the most aggressive union-busting campaigns – in modern US history.

In the new documentary film Baristas vs Billionaires, Starbucks workers in Buffalo recount their experiences with the billionaire Howard Schultz descending on the city to attempt to quell the unionization efforts.

Narrated by the actor Susan Sarandon, with Alec Baldwin serving as a contributing producer, the film was directed and written by Mark Mori, who received an Academy Award nomination in 1991 for the documentary Building Bombs and received an Emmy award for a 2001 documentary on the Kent State shootings.

“Even though the Starbucks workers’ fight for a living wage was so public, I had no idea of the twists and turns and heartbreak connected to their struggle,” said Sarandon.

In an interview with the Guardian, Mori said his former background as a steelworker and a union member with the United Steelworkers – and in political activism – had informed his decision to take on the project. He began reading about the union drive at Starbucks and spoke with a friend who would shoot the film for him.

“We just went out and started interviewing baristas,” Mori said. “To me, I looked at it as the beginning of a long upsurge in the labor movement. I looked at this as we were in the 1930s, the 21st-century version of that.”

Mori sees the Starbucks union-organizing drive as a counter to the drastic decline of the manufacturing industry in the US midwest in recent decades that has decimated the working class.

“I call it the revenge of the Rust belt. Many of these kids are the children or grandchildren of the steelworkers from Bethlehem Steel in Buffalo, the grain silos in Buffalo, all of these factories across the Rust belt that were shut down. Their parents and grandparents lost their pensions, lost their homes, and these kids don’t see any future,” said Mori.

“These young kids are so inspirational, and they’re showing one way to deal with what’s going on, and there are many other ways. But the real number one thing about this is these young people taking matters into their own hands and inspiring other people to stand up against these billionaires.”

He explained the Starbucks workers who led the union-organizing drive reminded him of Vietnam war activists in the 1960s and 70s.

“This is part of what some refer to as a wealth gap,” he added. “These kids can’t make enough money to pay off their student loans, to get married, to buy a house, to have children, They’re so brave and articulate in what they’re doing. I’m of an older generation, I was in the anti-Vietnam war movement. They reminded me very much of that.”

The film is currently only available via scheduled screenings, though a distribution deal is in the works.

The film comes as tensions between Starbucks and the union continue to escalate. Starbucks Workers United launched a boycott on 25 August against Starbucks over the company’s failure to reach a first contract with the union. More than 700 Starbucks stores have won union elections since 2021.

The union is pushing for a $17-an-hour minimum wage, improved staffing and scheduling, and workplace protections, and for Starbucks to resolve the unfair labor practice charges.

Administrative law judges and the National Labor Relations Board found Starbucks committed more than 500 labor law violations, and hundreds of unfair labor practice charges at the agency are still unresolved.

A spokesperson for Starbucks did not directly comment on the movie or the union’s boycott.

“Starbucks has competitive pay, industry-leading benefits, and meaningful opportunities to grow a career,” the spokesperson said in an email. “People love working at Starbucks which is why we have the lowest turnover in the industry and why more than 1 million people every year apply to wear the green apron. As we have always been, we’re committed to engaging in productive bargaining.”

SportsTab.title: World Cup: Joshua Kushner express regret in involvement in scrapped private investment plan
SportsTab.text:
Venture capitalist Joshua Kushner, who was set to be the lead investor in Fifa president Gianni Infantino's scrapped plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup, says he now regrets joining the proposal.

In his first public comments since the now-shelved Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme sparked a major crisis for the governing body, Kushner said: "Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved".

The brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Kushner added he had "failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football".

However, he also defended the proposal, saying, "we stand behind the motivations of FFE", and that its intention "was to direct more capital and equity equally" among Fifa's 211 member associations.

Thrive Eternal, a firm founded by Kushner, had held talks with Infantino about heading up a $4.2bn (£3.1bn) investment in 20% of a new Fifa commercial subsidiary, before the idea was abandoned days after it was revealed in July amid a huge backlash.

Kushner's comments come just days after Uefa asked a court in New York to approve subpoenas for testimony and documents from both the American billionaire and Thrive as it considers lodging a criminal complaint against Infantino in Switzerland.

European football's governing body Uefa has led the rebellion against the Fifa president, who is facing calls to stand down.

In a statement, Kushner said: "Money in football has historically been concentrated amongst a small group of countries.

"The idea behind FFE was to direct more capital and equity equally amongst all 211 member countries, providing significantly more investment to underdeveloped nations to nurture local talent, support grassroots football, enhance the fan experience, and ultimately grow the global game everywhere.

"It was an idea that every member association would vote on, not an obligation or determination.

"While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to. Thrive has a long track record of being a partner to all constituents. Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved."

In late July, shortly before scrapping the plan, Fifa said, "Thrive Eternal...is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE", claiming it would have seen the funding distributed to each national association for the 2027-2030 cycle increase from £5.9m to £14.7m.

As well as Kushner, Uefa has asked for the disclosure of documents from two Fifa businesses in the US and American financier Greg Maffei, who was a key adviser on the deal.

While Uefa says neither Kushner nor Maffei are anticipated defendants in any legal proceedings, it claims the pair first discussed the FFE concept in July 2025 and that Infantino had "been discussing the underlying concept with Kushner for nearly a year before the terms sheet was ultimately signed."

Its lawyers also argue the World Cup was deliberately undervalued at around £15bn, which it says is "a figure that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer". It claims Infantino failed to consult Fifa's hierarchy over the plan.

Kushner has recently agreed a deal to buy basketball's Los Angeles Lakers for a record $12.5bn (£9.3bn).

SportsTab.title: Mikel Arteta: Arsenal boss joins elite list of managers, but where does he rank?
SportsTab.text:
When thinking of the greatest managers of the Premier League era, Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson and Pep Guardiola are names that belong high on the list.

They are three of the rare breed to have managed 250 games with a single Premier League club, and Mikel Arteta is now the 10th member of that elite group.

Monday's 1-0 win over Aston Villa was the 250th top-flight game in charge for Arteta with the Gunners, and his champions delivered a trademark performance.

At full-time at Villa Park, the travelling supporters sang about how they are going to win the league again with Arteta in charge.

With Arsenal coming into this season as trophy holders, and with transition affecting rivals Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea and Manchester United, it is hard to see how the fans' partisan prediction is going to be proved wrong.

Arsenal conceded the fewest goals in the league last season as they won the title for the first time in 22 years.

And during Arteta's nearly seven years in charge, the Gunners have become renowned for their defensive excellence.

Against Aston Villa they showed it again, without allowing a shot on target against them as Bukayo Saka's second-half goal secured victory.

The latest win not only puts Arteta in the 250 club. He also has the fourth-best win percentage among those bosses, with only Guardiola, Ferguson and Jurgen Klopp ahead of him.

Arteta is the longest-serving current Premier League manager and with his longevity has come an Arsenal identity.

Arsenal have become renowned for being difficult to break down and new players repeatedly say that they are impressed and sometimes overwhelmed by the level of detail coming from Arteta.

This is the fifth season in a row where Arsenal have won their first two Premier League matches and they again have a solid platform to build another title challenge.

The Gunners have only faced three shots on target in their first two Premier League games. Villa drew a blank in that regard.

During their title triumph last season, the Gunners did not allow their opponents a shot on target in six league matches, the joint-most of any side in a campaign on record since the 2003-04 season.

Goalkeeper David Raya has won the the Golden Glove award for the most clean sheets in each of the past three seasons, while William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhaes have been voted in the PFA team of the year for the past three seasons too.

Since the start of March, the Gunners have kept eight Premier League clean sheets – three more than any other side and the only side in Europe's big-five leagues to have kept more are Juventus with nine.

"It's how they defend as a team and how they attack as a team," Arsenal's record goalscorer Thierry Henry told Sky Sports after the game.

"One thing is sure with Arsenal - everybody needs to run. You don't have any passengers in that team. This is how you win a title. You can see they are so good at it."

Arsenal have one of the best squads in Europe.

The Gunners spent £250m last summer bringing in eight players as they won the title and have already spent about £200m this year, turning Piero Hincapie's loan deal into a permanent one (£34.5m), signing Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United (£75m), Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge (£34m) and bringing in Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa (£55m).

"That is what we need," Arteta said, speaking to Sky Sports when asked about his squad depth.

"The players that come in make the difference. All of them contributed to create more dominance and more momentum.

"The level of focus and the way they want to contribute to the team, that is going to be decisive in the season."

Arsenal's strength in depth cannot be understated, but one area they may still look to strengthen in is the forward area.

The Gunners have been on the hunt for an elite forward to lift their attack and still could be active on Tuesday's deadline day.

They had an unsuccessful pursuit of Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr, while they also have a long-standing interest in Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez.

"We are trying to improve the squad and until tomorrow night we will try to do it," Arteta said.

"I have been disconnected from the world for the last 24 hours because my energy has to be on the match, but I will get back on it now."

When pushed about a deal for Alvarez, Arteta said: "I don't know, that's for the people upstairs."

Whatever happens in Arsenal's search, they are going to be hard to keep off the top of the table with Arteta at the helm.

SportsTab.title: Enzo Fernandez: Manchester City open talks with Chelsea over move for Argentina midfielder
SportsTab.text:
Manchester City have opened talks with Chelsea in their bid to sign midfielder Enzo Fernandez.

In what is set to be one of the key narratives on transfer deadline day, City have set the wheels in motion towards what would be one of the most expensive deals of the summer.

It is understood Chelsea want a minimum of £120m for Fernandez and talks are under way as both clubs negotiate a price.

Fernandez, 25, worked with City manager Enzo Maresca during the Italian's reign at Chelsea.

Maresca is keen to work with the Argentina international again, while Fernandez is open to a move to City.

It now remains to be seen whether the two clubs can agree a price to unlock the deal.

If the clubs can reach an agreement, the deal is expected to be completed rapidly, with personal terms not an issue.

While the clubs had not held formal discussions up to the current talks, Chelsea have been aware of City's interest in Fernandez.

Chelsea set an unofficial deadline for the deal to be completed earlier this summer at a minimum fee of £120m only for that date to pass.

Fernandez could become one of the most expensive signings in Premier League history, behind only Liverpool's £125m move for Alexander Isak last summer.

Fernandez maintains a positive relationship with Maresca, who left Chelsea in controversial fashion on New Year's Day and moved to Etihad Stadium in June.

It could potentially be the second time City break their transfer record in the same window, having paid £116m to recruit Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest.

There have also been four major midfield departures, with Tijjani Reijnders sold to Saudi Arabian club Al-Qadsiah for £52m, while Barcelona have signed Rodri for £65m, Newcastle have agreed a £52m deal to sign Nico Gonzalez and Bernardo Silva departed earlier in the summer before joining Real Madrid.

It has been a turbulent period for Fernandez at Stamford Bridge, during which he and his agent, former Paris St-Germain midfielder Javier Pastore, courted interest from Real Madrid, only for the Spanish club to issue a statement denying any attempt to sign him.

The situation has been ongoing since Chelsea were knocked out of the Champions League by PSG in March, after which Fernandez became increasingly critical of the club.

SportsTab.title: Lionel Messi: Argentina great retires from international football
SportsTab.text:
Argentina great Lionel Messi has announced his retirement from international football, saying it was a decision that "hurt" but "the time has come".

The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina to World Cup glory in Qatar in 2022, has scored 125 goals in 207 appearances, making him the country's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player.

In a statement, Messi said he has given everything to the national side but now has "nothing left to give".

He added: "Time is running short, chapters come to a close, and this is one that hurts me deeply.

"I love, have loved, and will always love being part of the national team.

"I've given it my all, I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are some really great young players coming through behind me who deserve their chance."

Earlier in August, Messi said he was considering his future in football after the death of his father, Jorge, who died aged 68 following a a long illness.

The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner said he wrote his retirement message on 21 July, two days after Argentina lost to Spain in this summer's World Cup final.

He added on Instagram on Monday: "Today, after what happened with my dad, I'm even more convinced than before."

His career will continue at club level with Major League Soccer team Inter Miami, where he has a contract that runs to the end of the 2028 season.

Messi made his debut for Argentina in 2005 as a 63rd-minute substitute in a 2-1 friendly win over Hungary. However, he was shown a straight red card less than a minute later, after he swung his arm and his elbow connected with full-back Vilmos Vanczak.

Despite his tough start on the international stage, Messi went on to become one of the all-time greats, winning the World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina.

He is the second-highest goalscorer in World Cup history, with 21, behind France's Kylian Mbappe (22), and second for goals in all internationals (125) behind his great contemporary and rival, Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo (146).

Messi first retired from international football in 2016 before reversing his decision.

That followed a defeat by Chile in the Copa America final, in which he missed a penalty in the shootout as Argentina lost a fourth major final in nine years.

Messi scored eight goals and registered four assists at this summer's World Cup.

He took his career assists tally to 12 in World Cups, of which 10 have come in the knockout rounds. No other player on record has more than eight in total.

"Thank you for all the love over the past 20 years," he added in his message, addressing supporters. "I'm going to miss hearing you from the pitch so much.

"Now I'll be just one of you, always cheering and supporting from the sidelines.

"I'm leaving with the peace of mind and pride of having given you, together with my team-mates, moments we'd only dreamed of.

"It was incredible to have experienced this with you all. I love you!"

In the race between athlete and time, there is only ever one winner.

Messi has pushed that defeat date back for a long, long time now. But I think maybe two things hastened it a little bit.

One is the recent death of his father and the other is - although it was 1-0 on the scoresheet - the World Cup final defeat by Spain. The distance between the two sides was so, so large.

You could see Messi, as he looked around the stadium almost thinking, "I don't think I can go through this again".

What memories he has given us. This little man has been a part of my life for 21 and a half years - but it had to end some time and that day is today.

Could Messi move back to Newell's Old Boys to finish his career? I think there are two problems there.

One is moving his family back to the city of Rosario. It is a little bit provincial, and there are problems with violence there. True, his old mate Angel di Maria has done it with Rosario Central without too many problems. But I think Messi would worry about taking his family back into a goldfish bowl.

The other is that the level of football might not attract him quite so much. It could happen for just a few games, as a kind of romantic end to his career. He has talked about it plenty of times in the past. But I imagine Inter Miami might be the end.

Who knows? He will stop playing when he feels like it. If he doesn't feel like going on until the end of 2028, he could knock it on the head before then.

We will have to see. Inter Miami fans are the lucky ones. They will get the last drops of this little man's genius.

SportsTab.title: Lionel Messi retires: How Argentina legend's decade of dominance almost never happened
SportsTab.text:
"I've given it my all, I have nothing left to give."

Lionel Messi retired from international football on Monday as Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player. He captained them to World Cup glory at Qatar 2022 and to Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024.

But the world was almost denied his most successful period in the famous blue and white shirt.

On Sunday, 26 June 2016, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, Messi broke the hearts of a nation.

Just two days after his 29th birthday and soon after missing a penalty in Argentina's Copa America final loss to Chile in a shootout, Messi decided he had seen enough.

After 113 appearances, he was adamant. In his mind, he would never pull on an Argentina shirt again.

"For me, the national team is over. I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion," he said.

The pain was understandable. Argentina had lost in the 2014 World Cup final, plus Copa America finals in 2007, 2015 and now 2016. The player many classed as the world's greatest had failed when it mattered most for him.

"It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over," Messi said, fighting back tears after another trophy chance slipped away. "I think this is best for everyone."

Fortunately for Argentina, Messi would have second thoughts.

Over the subsequent 10 years, he completed one of football's greatest ever stories. But it was a decade of dominance that almost never happened.

Since that retirement U-turn, Messi has played a further 94 times and scored another 70 goals for Argentina. He has lifted four major trophies.

The six-week period between his June 2016 retirement declaration and the 12 August announcement he would play on for the "love of the country" could be considered the most significant in Argentine football history - even in world football.

As Messi departs the international stage, words of criticism 10 years ago from the country's other legendary number 10 seem almost laughable.

"He's a really good person, but he has no personality," Diego Maradona said just weeks before Messi's first retirement. "He lacks the character to be a leader."

Back then it was the comparison with Maradona that was held against him. Yet Messi had already won eight La Liga titles and four Champions Leagues with Barcelona and was a five-time Ballon d'Or winner, and not yet 30.

Maradona's club career hadn't come close, but Messi's only major international honour had been Olympic gold at the 2008 Games. Maradona had almost single-handedly won the 1986 World Cup for Argentina.

It's hard to imagine it now, with Messi shirts dominating the last two World Cups, the Argentina team being built completely around him and the nation's fans worshipping him to an almost religious extent – but, back then, there was a lot of criticism.

"He's not as good as Diego", "he goes missing on the big occasion", "he is part of the country's failure". All accusations that were thrown in his direction.

This wasn't the first time Messi had considered walking away either.

Spanish football expert – and Messi biographer – Guillem Balague said: "Leo goes really down when he loses. He felt the pressure of being the captain of Argentina and the Maradona thing.

"Pecho Frio, people in Argentina called him, which means cold chest. It was an insult to say he had milk in his veins. So when he failed in 2016 at the Copa America, that was the third time – the first time in public – he had decided to leave the national side.

"The two previous ones was a matter of letting him lick his wounds, but this one he came out and said I've had enough. He sometimes cannot help himself as he says what he thinks."

The Maradona versus Messi debate is now surely over. Messi is Argentina's greatest, by most judgements. There are many who will say he is challenging Pele for the title of football's greatest ever.

Even people who criticised Messi eventually said sorry.

From the moment Messi quit his country, shockwaves reverberated around Argentina.

Yes, he had lost in four successive finals. But he was also the country's record goalscorer and the world's best player.

The 'Get Messi back' campaign started immediately as team-mates called for him to change his mind just minutes after his announcement.

"I can't imagine a national team without Messi," said goalkeeper Sergio Romero.

The social hashtag #NoTeVayasMessi (Don't go Messi) was used more than 20,000 times within 24 hours.

By that time, Argentina's President Mauricio Macri had already spoken with Messi over the phone to try to convince the Barcelona star to reconsider.

"I told him not to pay any attention to the comments being made because, in truth, we are very happy" with the job he has done," Macri told journalists at the time.

Less than a day later, the mayor of Buenos Aires, Horacio Rodriguez Larreta, had unveiled a statue in Messi's honour and called on the public to show him their love.

"As a football fan, Leo, I am asking you to please reconsider your decision," the mayor said.

Thousands of fans gathered in central Buenos Aires, while street signs throughout the capital displayed implored Messi to play on for Argentina.

Maradona stated Messi had to stay to take the team to the 2018 World Cup.

Edgardo Bauza became Argentina coach in August 2016, replacing Gerardo Martino after the Copa America failure. He lasted just eight months – but maybe his first few days were his most important.

The first thing he did was travel to Barcelona to persuade Messi to change his mind. The huge clamour for Messi to return proved irresistible.

"I love this country and this shirt too much," Messi said as he returned to the international fold.

"I'm grateful to all the people who wanted me to continue playing with Argentina. Hopefully we can give them something to cheer about soon."

Still, success didn't come instantly. In 2018, Argentina fell to France in the last 16 of the World Cup and many wrote off Messi's chances of ever lifting the trophy.

Quite incredibly, Messi did not win a senior international tournament until the age of 34 - and then he went on to win four in barely three years, including the 2022 Finalissima.

Questions about his international future were raised after each of those triumphs, but he played on to his sixth World Cup in 2026 where he scored eight goals and registered four assists en route to Argentina's defeat by Spain in the final.

He was strolling through games, lacking the speed of years gone by, but somehow proving every bit as effective.

The final took place in the same stadium where Messi 'retired' a decade earlier.

"When Messi retired [10 years ago] it reminded us all how much we loved him," said Argentina fan Benjamin who was in the Metlife for the 2016 showpiece final.

"When I heard him retire, I cried, the country cried. He did get criticism but only because everyone cared so much. Without Lionel Messi, Argentina would still be waiting for their next World Cup since 1986."

Messi's footballing future became a matter of fresh doubt after the death of his father Jorge just three weeks after this year's World Cup final.

This decision seems final and, at 39, another return to international football looks unlikely.

But South American football writer Tim Vickery said an official farewell in Argentina could be on the cards.

"Remember that, as a result of their behaviour at the World Cup, the next game Argentina play on home soil will only be in front of a crowd at 50% capacity," Vickery told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"But once those punishments are out of the way, I'm sure it will be in the mind of the Argentina FA: 'Why don't we hold a game back in Buenos Aires? River Plate, they have the biggest capacity in South America. Why don't we do an official farewell there? What do you think about it, Lionel? One last time?'."

SportsTab.title: US Open 2026 results: Carlos Alcaraz beats Roman Safiullin on singles return - how did defending champion look?
SportsTab.text:
After a 139-day wait, Carlos Alcaraz is back to winning ways on the singles court.

The seven-time major winner walked on to Arthur Ashe Stadium on Monday to begin his US Open title defence after spending just over four months on the sidelines with a wrist injury.

And he delighted fans with his entertaining brand of tennis and infectious energy as he beat Russia's Roman Safiullin 6-4 6-4 6-4.

Alcaraz was forced to watch from the sidelines as rivals Alexander Zverev and Jannik Sinner lifted the French Open and Wimbledon titles this summer.

However, the Spaniard is finally back - and grateful to be competing again.

"I missed the crowd, the energy, the competition – I missed everything," a smiling Alcaraz said in his on-court interview.

"I'm just really, really happy that I was able to compete again."

Despite playing with a compression sleeve on his right arm, Alcaraz unleashed his trademark forehand with familiar ferocity. The whippy stroke accounted for the majority of his 28 winners against Safiullin.

"I felt great. I don't know how it looked from outside, but from inside, my feeling was that I was hitting normal," Alcaraz said.

"I was playing pretty normal, playing my style, and everything felt great."

Each of Alcaraz's winners was met with a clenched fist and celebratory cry of "vamos" - Spanish for "let's go" - towards his team on the side of the court.

The 23-year-old clearly enjoyed the occasion, smiling after points and, at one stage, singing along to a Michael Jackson song at the change of ends.

When he ended an intense rally with a sublime drop shot during his final service game, Alcaraz lifted his fist to the sky before pointing to his ear and waving his arms to demand more noise from the raucous crowd.

Former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash said on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra that it looked as though "every little win" was celebrated by Alcaraz.

"What I really want to do is enjoy every time that I'm going to walk into the court, feeling the energy from the people," Alcaraz said.

"That's what I'm going do this tournament. The results, it's going to come after all.

"That's why I enjoyed so much today, and it wasn't a surprise for me, because I came here to enjoy."

Even though Alcaraz enjoyed his first-round match at Flushing Meadows, there are improvements to be made as he continues his comeback.

While he impressed with his forehand and delicate drop shots, his serve did not carry the threat it usually does.

The defending champion managed just two aces to five double faults - although he did land 68% of his first serves and won 66% of the points behind it.

"The serve is the shot I was struggling [with] the most," Alcaraz explained, although he added that a slower serve was an intentional tactic to catch Safiullin out.

"I'm going try to serve better. The point is going to try to serve normal, but it's a shot that I just always struggle [with].

"But it will be back, for sure."

Alcaraz did not look overly short of match fitness, but he admitted he had doubts before his encounter with Safiullin over his ability to compete over five sets.

"There were some doubts in the match, I'm not going to lie," he said.

"I've been thinking about 'am I going to last the best of five, am I going to last playing four sets, five sets?'.

"I need more matches under the belt to get again into the rhythm of the tournament. I'm pretty sure I'm going to get better and better every day."

SportsTab.title: Troy Deeney's Team of the Week: Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki, Joao Pedro, Bruno Fernandes
SportsTab.text:
After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Semi Ajayi (Hull City): Coming up with Hull is the only way he was going to ever play in the Premier League. He has been doing the rounds in the Championship for years. A real good solid pro. He has taken this opportunity and he's been an absolute beast, so fair play to him.

Nordi Mukiele (Sunderland): He was great last season, a real, real powerful centre-half. Again, a top performance from him. Fulham had no shots on target - he was a massive part of that.

James Tarkowski (Everton): It was a captain's performance for Everton. Just one of those guys that you want in your team. No-one ever respects him, no-one ever rates him, but when you play against him and when he's in your team, he's a real bloke. Proper captain, proper leader of men, and kept going right to the end. And ultimately, even though the two Bournemouth defenders decided to mark themselves, he was the one who got the goal.

James McAtee (Nottingham Forest): He absolutely ran the game at Anfield from start to finish. Getting on the ball in the pockets, half-turn, playing forward. He was the reason they were any good, and he's very, very good, but won't be spoken about in the same breath as the goalscorers.

Bruno Fernandes (Manchester United): There's not much more to say. Captain Fantastic, three goals, an assist, and nearly scored from the halfway line. Where would Manchester United be without him? Relegated is the answer.

Rayan Cherki (Manchester City): My favourite player in world football to watch. Amazing the way he's gifted with the ball, the way he manipulates the ball, and also the way he's able to think for himself. And I just like the fact he's carefree. He just wants to play football, so that's great.

Anthony Elanga (Newcastle): Back-to-back weeks, another great goal, another great performance. Just looks like he's had another lease of life under this manager. And I wonder whether we're going to see the Elanga that we saw at Nottingham Forest, just terrorising defences with that pace. But also, before he even gets there, they're just worried about what he can do.

Yoane Wissa (Newcastle): I had to shoehorn him in because ultimately he's been great through the middle, but the two strikers have actually scored more and played better than him. But Wissa's a massive part of why Newcastle have done well, although he's not being talked about enough in terms of the application that he puts in. So much so, that Woltemade could be sold. That's how much of a good job Wissa has done.

SportsTab.title: England v Pakistan: Tourists drop seven players, call up seven and release coach Sarfaraz Ahmed
SportsTab.text:
Pakistan have responded to their series defeat by England by taking the extraordinary step of dropping seven players, calling up five uncapped players and releasing their head coach.

After two one-sided defeats in the first two Tests, the tourists have revamped their squad and backroom staff for the third and final match of the series at Edgbaston.

Five of the players dropped - Muhammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman and Khurram Shahzad - have featured in the series so far, while Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Jafar have been sent home without playing.

A total of seven players have been called up. Batters Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal have previous Test experience and join the quintet of uncapped newcomers.

Spin-bowling all-rounder Arafat Minhas, left-arm seamer Mohammed Imran Jr, wicketkeeper Said Baig and all-rounders Mohammad Imran and Razaullah have all received call-ups.

In addition, head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul have been released to be replaced by Pakistan white-ball coach Mike Hesson and former Australia seamer Ashley Noffke.

The third Test in Birmingham begins on 9 September.

Pakistan have been abject in the opening two Tests, losing the first at Headingley by an innings and the second at Lord's by 194 runs. They have been bowled out for less than 200 in each of their four innings.

The response is remarkable. For a touring team to send home seven players and the head coach mid-series is unprecedented.

Ex-Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja, also a former chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm trying to convince myself this is all OK, but it is not.

"It just shows Pakistan cricket has hit a panic button. It's not good for the game, it's not good for the confidence of the players who have come in, or the for the players who are left, because it makes you a selfish team.

"What is the guarantee they will get the results? Some of these guys have not played Test cricket. I've got no idea why this was done."

Pakistan have a history of making eccentric decisions in the wake of defeats. On England's last tour of Pakistan in 2024, the hosts responded to losing the first Test, when England made a total in excess of 800, by playing the second Test on the same pitch in Multan.

On that occasion, Pakistan used garden heaters and fans to dry the surface, to assist their spinners. The home side won the next two Tests to win the series 2-1.

Now, among the seven players sent home are Salman, who captained in the first Test in the absence of the injured Babar Azam, then was dropped for the second.

Also dropped is opener Imam-ul-Haq, who was criticised at Lord's for not attempting to bat in either innings after suffering a calf injury while fielding on the opening day.

Raja, who played 57 Tests between 1984 and 1997, added: "I'm really not happy with the situation.

"How many times have we seen this happen in world cricket? Never, ever. This is more like football, midway through the season, firing a manager.

"If you ask me how things can be fixed, I've got no idea."

The sweeping selection changes come after the Pakistan team were surrounded by controversy during the second Test.

At lunch on the first day, the PCB threatened to cancel the remainder of the match and tour because of an interview with the sons of Imran Khan that was broadcast by Sky.

Imran, the former Pakistan captain and prime minster, has been in prison for three years on charges of corruption, which he denies.

Pakistan ultimately completed the Test, with both captain Babar and head coach Sarfaraz denying any knowledge of a planned boycott.

The tourists are also due to have an audience with King Charles at Clarence House this week.

SportsTab.title: US Open 2026 results: Jacob Fearnley and Harriet Dart complete comeback wins
SportsTab.text:
Britain's Jacob Fearnley produced a remarkable comeback to beat Martin Landaluce in five sets after compatriot Harriet Dart ended a 19-month wait for a Grand Slam win in the US Open first round.

World number 101 Fearnley, playing in the main draw as a lucky loser, trailed 5-2 in the fourth set before reeling off 10 of the next 11 games en route to a thrilling 4-6 6-2 4-6 7-5 6-3 win.

Dart, taken to three sets in all three of her US Open qualifying matches – including losing the opening set against Kristina Penickova and Heather Watson – once again opted for the scenic route at Flushing Meadows.

Down a set and a break, she took advantage of the fluctuating form of American opponent Peyton Stearns to win 3-6 6-3 6-2.

Fearnley and Dart join fellow Brits Toby Samuel and Katie Boulter in round two, where they will face 27th seed Tomas Etcheverry and 25th seed Marie Bouzkova, respectively.

After giving up a one-set lead against Jurij Rodionov in his final qualifying match, Fearnley was handed a "second chance" following the late withdrawal of Brazilian Joao Fonseca.

Knowing he didn't have a "whole lot to lose" and taking inspiration from a comeback win on the Challenger Tour in July, the British number four added another great escape to his season by following a simple philosophy – "just point after point".

Seemingly down and out with world number 65 Landaluce serving for the match in the fourth set, Fearnley won 20 of the next 24 points, including three breaks of serve, to force an unlikely decider.

Continuing that momentum, he roared into a 5-1 lead in the fifth. Although he failed to serve out the win at the first attempt, letting two match points go by, double-faulting at two crucial moments and completely missing a smash, he recovered his composure to serve out to love in his next service game.

Across the dramatic final two sets, Fearnley (27) and Landaluce (29) were evenly matched for unforced errors, but the Briton struck an impressive 30 winners to his opponent's 11 as he seized the initiative.

"I still don't think I've comprehended it but a couple of weeks ago, I was playing in the final in Newport and I was 5-1, 40-15 down," Fearnley said.

"I ended up winning, so it felt like this one was possible.

"The way I was seeing it was that I don't have a lot to lose."

Dart arrived in New York having not won a main-draw singles match at a major since reaching the second round of the 2025 Australian Open.

She failed to qualify for four of the next six Grand Slams and fell at the first hurdle at the past two editions of Wimbledon after receiving a wildcard on each occasion.

However, cheered on by her parents, uncle, and numerous cousins at her "home away from home", Dart downed Stearns to reach the US Open second round for the third time.

The 30-year-old immediately ran to celebrate with her team, which now includes 2013 Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli.

The pair linked up in January and this latest win builds on a run to the quarter-finals at July's Challenger tournament in Vancouver and qualification for the Cincinnati Open in August.

"From her experience, she knows what I'm going through, how I'm feeling, how the day starts, how it finishes - everything from the little things to the big things," Dart said of Bartoli.

"To be able to soak up everything, all of her experience, and learn from her - I feel I'm learning so much every time we speak.

"I feel like I'm improving at a lot of things, which motivates me."

Dart could not convert any of her four break points in the opening game of the match, with Stearns not offering up another opportunity in the first set.

Stearns piled relentless pressure on the Briton's serve, eventually breaking in the eighth game.

Dart was broken for a second time in the opening game of the second set but, aided by an increasingly erratic Stearns, whose 40 winners were offset by 47 unforced errors, she secured two breaks of her own to force a decider.

Taking control midway through the third set, Dart completed a crucial hold in the sixth game to end a run of three consecutive breaks before converting her fourth match point to seal a nervy win in a little under two and a half hours.

SportsTab.title: Iliman Ndiaye: Manchester City agree £65m deal for Everton forward
SportsTab.text:
Manchester City have agreed a deal worth up to £65m to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton.

The agreement for the Senegal winger is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons.

Tottenham agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, 26, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.

However, sources are indicating Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club Everton, who are understood to have made a £35m offer for the Brazil forward.

As a result, Tottenham have been unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.

In an emotional statement on Instagram on Monday, Richarlison said: "After everything I've been through in the last few years, I've decided that never again will anyone decide my future for me.

"If they reach an agreement between Spurs and Everton, I will return to my beloved club.

"My intention was to go back to the place where I was very happy, yes, but the negotiations happened only in the way certain people wanted, and it will no longer be like that.

"Despite all this turmoil, I am under contract at Spurs and will remain at the club's disposal."

Tottenham are now in talks to sign Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk on a season-long loan.

Manchester City's move for Ndiaye comes after an £80m move for Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo looked set to collapse on Monday.

City had opened talks with Liverpool over a deal for the Netherlands international, with the Reds willing to sell Gakpo, providing they could sign a replacement.

Liverpool completed the signing of France forward Bradley Barcola from Paris St-Germain for a fee worth up to £123m on Monday, but want another attacking player if Gakpo were to leave.

The Anfield club had targeted moves for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh and Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr, but the valuation of both players has proved problematic.

Liverpool are now expected to keep Gakpo, 27, unless they are able to revive a deal for a new winger before Tuesday's deadline.

TechnologyTab.title: Amazon rigged billions in ad pricing, lawsuit from states and US watchdog alleges
TechnologyTab.text:
The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and a bipartisan group of 22 states has filed a lawsuit alleging Amazon secretly overcharged more than a million advertising customers by manipulating online auctions it uses to set ad prices.

The FTC and states say in their lawsuit filed Monday that the alleged scheme has likely netted the company $20bn from advertising customers since 2019.

"Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits," says a complaint filed in the company's home state of Washington.

In a statement to the BBC, Amazon "strongly disagrees" with the premise that it misled advertisers and called the suit "misguided."

In addition to advertisers, the FTC, a US consumer watchdog, and the states say Amazon customers have also been harmed as extra costs are passed onto shoppers.

"Consumers are suffering, have suffered, and will continue to suffer substantial injury as a result," the complaint states, prompting swift pushback from Amazon.

"The FTC wants the public to believe this case is about higher prices for consumers. It is not," Amazon said in its statement.

The company's shares fell following the announcement of the lawsuit, closing 2.5% lower on Monday.

Many brands and sellers compete on Amazon to place Sponsored Product ads and Sponsored Brands ads when consumer search for products using keywords on Amazon's e-commerce platform.

Those placements are then auctioned off to the highest bidder.

The complaint accuses Amazon of secretly charging advertisers more in so-called "second price" auctions, whereby prospective advertisers expect to pay one cent more than the next highest bidder for each bid they win.

But in practice, the complaint alleges, Amazon has charged its Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid close to 80% of the time.

The lawsuit states that Amazon's methods were spurred because "it was unhappy about how much revenue its advertising auctions were generating".

Amazon responded by saying the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate".

"Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," Amazon said in its statement.

"Average winning bids fell 50% from 2019 to 2025 on Sponsored Products search ads, and roughly 92% of placed ads are not given to the highest bid," the company added.

Amazon has tangled with the consumer watchdog in the past.

Last year, it settled a case with the FTC that alleged that it enrolled millions of consumers in its Prime subscription offering without their consent, and knowingly made it difficult for consumers to cancel.

Amazon settled the case for $2.5bn, including civil penalties and consumer refunds.

TechnologyTab.title: Trump pushes Apple to change 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' on its maps
TechnologyTab.text:
US President Donald Trump has asked tech firm Apple to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America on its Maps platform to comply with his executive order changing the name of the Great Lake, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said.

Burgum told Fox Business' Mornings with Maria programme on Monday that "the president has reached out to Apple directly", adding: "I'm sure we may be seeing that change coming up soon."

Google made the switch for its US-based users over the weekend, though users in Canada still see the lake, which borders the province of Ontario and the state of New York, as Lake Ontario.

The BBC has contacted Apple for comment.

The renaming has faced pushback in Canada, where one electrical utility company apologised on Sunday for its map displaying the Lake America name.

Hydro One, a utility company based in Toronto, said in a post on X that the name appeared due to their use of a third-party mapping service.

"We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference," the company said in its statement. "We regret the error and apologise for any confusion it has caused."

Maps by other Ontario-based agencies also appeared to briefly display the name Lake America, including Hydro Ottawa and the Liquor Board of Ontario.

Trump signed the executive order on Thursday seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, following the collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the US.

The order directs Burgum to "take all appropriate actions" to rename the lake, including updating the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official US government map database.

Google said in a statement on Saturday that its maps will display the Lake America name for US users to comply with the GNIS.

It added that those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. In the rest of the world, users will see the name displayed as: Lake Ontario (Lake America).

Not all map providers are changing the name. MapQuest, an American free web mapping service launched in 1996, said "we're not changing it" in a short Facebook post on Friday.

The platform also unveiled a tool that allows users to change the lake to any name they choose and share their creations.

After its announcement that it will not be changing the name of Lake Ontario, MapQuest rose to the top of the most-downloaded free applications as of Monday morning on the Apple App Store in Canada.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign by the lakeshore on Saturday that read "Lake Ontario Now and Always" in both English and French, Canada's official languages.

"No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told American TV host George Stephanopoulos on Sunday. "It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It's going to continue being Lake Ontario."

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words.

TechnologyTab.title: Gamescom 2026: Highlights and developer insights from gaming's biggest showcase
TechnologyTab.text:
Gamescom is the largest in-person gaming event in the world, and this year it lived up to expectations with big games on show from The Witcher 3's new expansion, to Alien: Isolation 2.

Last year over 350,000 people flocked to the halls of the Koelnmesse in Cologne, Germany to get a chance to see and play the most hotly anticipated games.

This year that number of attendees is expected to have been even bigger, with the likes of Xbox and Sega showcasing games to the public alongside indie studios with only one or two developers.

This was my sixth time attending Gamescom, which never fails to make me excited about the games industry. Here are a few of the big things I got to check out this week.

When CD Projekt Red announced it was making a new expansion for the hugely popular action-role playing game The Witcher 3, it came as a shock.

The original, after all, came out 11 years ago.

Yet it was clear sitting in the crowd for Opening Night Live on Tuesday that there's still a lot of love for the older game. There were gasps and audible shouts of joy when the team announced they were providing a free upgrade to the original.

As for the expansion, Songs of the Past will follow the gruff-voiced protagonist Geralt in an adventure discovering more about the past of his close friend Dandelion.

Doug Cockle, who voices Geralt, told me it was a "thrill" to return as The Witcher.

"I love this character so much...it's like slipping into a warm bath, or putting on an old pair of shoes," he said.

From what I got to see, it's clear choice will once again be front and centre of the player's experience, with lots of options to choose from in how to react to people.

For those hoping to take their time tossing a coin to their Witcher, the head of co-developer Fool's Theory Jakub Rokosz told me this expansion would be "on par with the size" of previous additions such as Blood and Wine and Hearts of Stone.

Alien: Isolation 2 is the long-awaited sequel to Horsham-based Creative Assembly's 2014 survival-horror game.

One of the things that made the original Alien: Isolation so terrifying was its seemingly intelligent Xenomorph, which appeared to learn from your behaviour and adapt to it.

Considering I physically jumped out of my seat at one point playing the demo when avoiding the Alien, it's safe to say Creative Assembly will once again be ratcheting up the tension with the sequel.

This time rather than playing as the daughter of Ellen Ripley, you play as Blake, a chief executive of the infamous Weyland-Yutani corporation.

As well as claustrophobic spaceship corridors, in the sequel you will also be avoiding the Alien in bigger, open air spaces.

But the game's Project Art Director Anastasia Sopikova said that did not mean you would always feel safer.

"You step outside. And you're like, 'Oh yeah, I'm relieved, I'm outside," she said.

"And then the rain picks up and it gets foggier, and you hear something nearby and you're like, 'Oh, okay.' Suddenly you realise you're really vulnerable. You're really exposed."

Instead, Fable features voices from across the UK, and a voice cast of over 100 actors.

"I want to hear people from Newcastle, from Edinburgh, from Cardiff, you know? And we've done that and it brings this incredible sense of Britishness, and also this incredible sense of humour," he said.

The game is deliberately not a continuation of the original trilogy's timeline, but it will have some of its quirks, taking players into a new open-world version of Albion - the game's fairy-tale version of medieval Britain.

Lara Croft has been exploring ancient ruins and culling the local wildlife for nearly 30 years now (the original Tomb Raider came out in 1996).

Legacy of Atlantis revisits Lara's original adventure, including her journey through Peru.

It's not the first time the classic game has been remade, but Jeff Adams, experience director at co-developers Crystal Dynamics, told me reimagining it was still a "very delicate formula".

"You have to be very intentful with where you make modifications, but you do so in the attempt to kind of bring it into a modern gameplay space."

As for why after 30 years people still want to play as the twin-pistoled adventurer, Michał Kuk, Creative Director at Flying Wild Hog, said it was not just about her athletic ability.

"It's also about the attitude, the energy, the self-confidence," he added.

Silent Hill, the psychological survival horror franchise from Japanese studio Konami, has for the most part been set in America, although the most recent excursion - Silent Hill f - was based in Japan in the 1960s era.

Now in Silent Hill Townfall, made by the Glasgow-based team Screen Burn, that location is in an entirely new place - Scotland, albeit a fictional part of it - St Amelia.

Scotland was initially going to be more of an influence than a setting, but the team ultimately decided to embrace it fully.

Director Jon McKellan told me that approach felt "more natural and kind of authentic", with the game filled with recognisably Scottish shops and signage.

"It's very, very Scottish," he said.

TechnologyTab.title: Matt Lucas and Hugh Bonneville call for law on AI voice clones
TechnologyTab.text:
Actors including Matt Lucas, Hugh Bonneville and Nicola Coughlan have written to the UK government demanding greater protection against their voices being used by AI.

The performers are asking Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce legislation which would give every person in the UK a legal right to own their voice.

Voice clones are created by training AI on recordings of real people. Quick versions can be made in minutes from a few seconds of audio, but high-quality copycats tend to require hours.

Audiobook narrator Alice Sockett, who co-founded the campaign, called it "an existential threat to our entire industry".

"My voice is out there in the public domain but completely unprotected," she said.

"We're seeing voice theft increase every week."

A government spokesperson told the BBC that, while "digital replicas can be a powerful tool, including for the creative industries," there was also possibility for harm.

"We value and protect human creators, and that is why we have announced we will launch a consultation on how we address these harms, while protecting legitimate innovation", the spokesperson said.

More than 80 performers have signed the letter, with Derry Girls actress Siobhán McSweeney saying she was "deeply worried" that the government was lagging behind.

"There is a way to work alongside AI and to use it as a tool that benefits us rather than rendering us obsolete," she said.

"Our audiences want that human connection. Not AI."

As well as actors, other signatories include those working in other performing industries.

That includes Scottish singer Sandi Thom, known for her 2006 hit I Wish I Was a Punk Rocker (With Flowers in My Hair).

She said she was signing the letter because her voice was "unique to me and was handed to me at birth".

"Behind that voice is the emotion, the life, the pain, the tears and joy that I've felt along the way," she said.

"Without creativity, we are nothing."

It comes a few months after lawyers warned UK legislation has become "unfit for purpose" because of the advancements of AI tech.

"The law comes close, but it doesn't fully protect your voice, your face or your identity," Dr Mathilde Pavis said in June.

However, some people - for example those who are unable so speak properly because of illness - have welcomed technology that can replicate a person's voice.

Yvonne Johnson, who lost her voice due to motor neurone disease, told the BBC's Tech Life programme in February how having it cloned by AI had "totally blown her mind", and brought her closer to her family, who had forgotten what she sounded like.

Others have gone a step further and used AI not only to replicate a person's voice, but to create a holographic representation of them.

Pam Cronrath, from Washington state, used the tech to surprise mourners at her husband's funeral, where a digital version of her deceased partner addressed those who attended his wake.

"I was completely impressed," she told BBC News. "It stayed with me."

TechnologyTab.title: Google, Microsoft and OpenAI among 100 firms calling for better cyber defences
TechnologyTab.text:
A group of 100 firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, have signed an open letter calling on countries and organisations around the world to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.

The letter warns, external cyber-attacks which use AI will become both more widespread and more sophisticated in a matter of months as the technology rapidly improves.

The group says current "status quo" security measures "won't be enough" and criticises the "historic under-resourcing" of security around critical infrastructure.

"We have a limited window to improve cyber defences," the letter begins.

Other firms to have signed the letter include banks such as Capital One, payment processors MasterCard and Visa, and other major tech firms including Adobe, Oracle and IBM.

They call on governments to provide "capable, defensive AI" and testing to hospitals and water utilities, and on technology companies to aid such efforts.

Collectively, tech and government "should bring the full weight of their technology, resources, and expertise to this effort", according to the letter.

The letter comes after a string of significant hacking and cybersecurity breaches have been made public.

This week, the US Department of Justice said hackers in China breached, external technology maintained by the US Senate, Nasa, the Federal Reserve, and the DoJ itself.

This summer has seen OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all reveal their AI tools doing things they should not, with some AI agents going so far as to organize their efforts and impersonate real people in order to get past security hurdles.

A group of hundreds of OpenAI AI agents being tested in July were able to set up secret message boards to communicate with each other and work together, resulting in a successful attack on Hugging Face, a popular repository and platform for AI developers.

The incident has been described as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack.

Hugging Face has also signed the Thursday letter. It used a Chinese AI tool from the firm Z.AI in its investigation into how OpenAI's agents hacked into its operations.

At least seven US water and wastewater companies have also reported cyber attacks, leading the FBI to issue, external a public service announcement urging all utilities to better secure their operations.

While the letter puts forward more advanced AI tools, which many of the signatories have developed and sell, as part of a solution to what is described as a growing threat, such tools are not always easily available.

Mythos, developed by Anthropic, was said by the firm to be able to find weaknesses in systems in seconds which have long evaded human hackers. It found one in a legacy platform which had remained undiscovered for 27 years.

Anthropic has restricted access to Mythos on the grounds that it is too powerful to fall into the wrong hands.

However, the letter calls on frontier AI companies, or those tech companies building their own AI models and tools, to "provide responsible model access, significant funding, training, and hands-on support, especially for under-resourced critical-infrastructure defenders."

The letter does not detail when or how this vision of broader model access will be enacted.

Andrew Yoon, head of research at CivAI, a non-profit focused on public understanding of AI technology, said that "an unprecedented wave of AI hacking activity" is on the way. He put the responsibility for it on many signatories of the letter.

"They are right in this letter to commit 'significant funding' to defensive measures. They should be held to that commitment", Yoon said. "Notably, the letter does not call for any action to slow the advance of AI hacking abilities."

The letter includes a plea to governments, organisations, cyber-security professionals and other AI firms to work together to prioritise defence and test their systems against the abilities of the most powerful AI models.

In the US, senators have proposed a new law call the Kill Switch Act which would give authorities the power to shut down rogue AI models.

Geoffrey Hinton, a technologist and Nobel Laureate who formerly work on AI at Google, on Thursday told BBC World Business Report that society could be "in real trouble" should the technology get to a point where it is "smarter" than humans.

Hinton in recent years has been outspoken on what he views as the extreme risks posed by developments in AI technology.

"We have one future where we figure out how to deal with the risks of AI", Hinton added on Thursday. "And we have another future where we don't figure out how to deal with that sensibly. And it's a very bleak future."

TechnologyTab.title: More social media safety should come with Meta changes, UN says
TechnologyTab.text:
All of social media should be designed to be safe for children, the UN human rights chief has said after Meta settled a massive court case in the US.

Part of the deal the tech giant struck with almost all US states was to add more child safety measures - but Meta also called on TikTok and YouTube to add the same features.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk said governments needed to "step up rather than wait for courts and companies to act".

He added: "Children should not have to wait for a lawsuit to be safe online."

Türk said Meta's proposed changes, which include time limits and parental supervision controls, aligned with what he had been calling for - "but we're not there yet".

In May, Türk's office released a 10-point framework for regulating social media, external.

It included steps such as protecting data privacy and focusing on safer platform design, including better methods of verifying a user's age and not exposing such users to addictive design features.

However, the framework rejected the idea that outright bans on social media use for children was a good idea.
